heroIntro: In Bangladesh property transfers governed by Muslim Personal Law, two instruments are widely utilized: 'Simple Hiba' (Gift) and 'Heba-bil-Ewaz' (Gift with Consideration). Despite their common use, many landowners and heirs fail to understand their profound legal divergence. While a simple Hiba is a voluntary transfer of property made purely out of natural love and affection without any exchange, a Heba-bil-Ewaz requires an actual, genuine 'Ewaz' or return gift—such as a prayer mat, a copy of the Holy Quran, or a token monetary sum. Crucially, while simple gifts may be revocable under limited conditions, a Heba-bil-Ewaz operates under the legal fiction of a sale contract and cannot be revoked unilaterally once executed. Senior Supreme Court Advocate Md. Shah Alam breaks down statutory registration fees, the evidentiary requirements of Ewaz, and the exact judicial procedure to annul fraudulent gift deeds in civil court under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. quickAnswer.heading: ⚡ Key Legal Distinctions: Simple Hiba vs Heba-bil-Ewaz
points: A Simple Hiba is an unconditional gift without any return consideration. A Heba-bil-Ewaz is a reciprocal gift made expressly in exchange for another valuable item (Ewaz).
Two absolute prerequisites must be proven for Heba-bil-Ewaz: (1) Actual, genuine delivery of the return consideration (Ewaz), and (2) The donor's bona fide intention to divest ownership.
Under Section 78B of the Registration Act 1908, gifts among blood relatives qualify for a fixed nominal fee of BDT 100, whereas gifts to non-relatives attract full ad-valorem stamp duty and taxes.
A completed Heba-bil-Ewaz CANNOT be revoked unilaterally by the donor through a cancellation deed. Any revocation requires a decree from a competent Civil Court.
Lawsuits challenging fraudulent or fabricated Heba deeds must be filed within 3 years of discovery under Article 91 of the Limitation Act 1908.

sections.h2: 1. The Juridical Definition of Heba-bil-Ewaz in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Under classical Islamic jurisprudence as recognized by Bangladesh courts, Heba-bil-Ewaz represents a composite transaction: it begins as a gift and ripens into a sale. When a donor presents land to a recipient and the recipient tenders a return consideration (Ewaz), the transaction is legally transformed.

The Supreme Court of Bangladesh in numerous decisions has reiterated that in order for a Heba-bil-Ewaz to be legally valid, the return consideration must be actual, bona fide, and delivered prior to or concurrently with the execution of the instrument. Merely mentioning a symbolic return in the deed text without genuine delivery will render the instrument vulnerable to legal challenge.

sections.h2: 2. The 4 Fundamental Differences Between Simple Hiba and Heba-bil-Ewaz
sections.content:
Legal ParameterSimple Hiba (Unconditional Gift)Heba-bil-Ewaz (Gift for Return)
1. Consideration (Ewaz)None. Purely motivated by love, affection, or religious merit.Mandatory delivery of a valuable reciprocal gift.
2. Judicial TreatmentPure gift under Transfer of Property Act.Treated judicially as a contract of sale (Baye).
3. Delivery of PossessionStrict physical delivery (Qabdah) is mandatory to complete title.Possession transfer is formal; reciprocal Ewaz solidifies title.
4. RevocabilityRevocable under narrow conditions prior to delivery or blood bar.Completely irrevocable once consideration and deed coalesce.

sections.h2: 3. Official Sub-Registry Fees Under Section 78B Registration Act
sections.content:
The government of Bangladesh provides statutory tax incentives for familial gifts under Section 78B of the Registration Act, 1908:

  • Blood-Relation Gift Deeds (Between spouses, parents, children, full siblings, grandparents, grandchildren): Statutory registration fee is capped at a flat BDT 100, with BDT 300 affidavit stamp and nominal processing fees (totaling roughly BDT 1,200 to 1,500). No local government tax or ad-valorem stamp duty applies.
  • Non-Relative Gifts & External Heba-bil-Ewaz: If transferred outside statutory blood categories, the instrument is assessed as an ordinary conveyance attracting 1.5% Stamp Duty, 1% Registration Fee, 3% Local Government Tax, and source taxes.

sections.h2: 4. Can a Donor Unilaterally Cancel a Registered Heba Deed?
sections.content:
A critical misconception among landowners is that a donor who regrets executing a gift deed can simply return to the Sub-Registry Office and execute a 'Cancellation Deed' (দলিল বাতিলকরণ). The Supreme Court has unequivocally ruled that unilateral cancellation deeds are nullities.

Once a registered conveyance transfers title, the registering officer becomes functus officio. The donor cannot divest the grantee of ownership without an adversarial decree from a court of competent civil jurisdiction. Any unilateral revocation deed will be disregarded by Land Offices during mutation hearings.

sections.h2: 5. Protecting Daughters and Sisters Against Fraudulent Gift Transfers
sections.content:
A frequent abusive practice in rural and urban Bangladesh involves male siblings forging a father's thumbprint on a Heba-bil-Ewaz deed shortly before his death to deprive female heirs of their rightful Quranic shares. Aggrieved female heirs must act swiftly:

  1. Obtain Certified Copies: Apply immediately for certified copies (নকল) from the Sub-Registry Office.
  2. Forensic Handwriting Analysis: Apply to the civil court for appointment of a CID Forensic Handwriting Expert under Section 73 of the Evidence Act to inspect the contested signature.
  3. File Mutation Objections: Lodge written caveats with the Assistant Commissioner (Land) to stay separate Khatian mutations based on the questionable deed.

sections.h2: 6. Instituting a Cancellation Lawsuit Under Section 39 Specific Relief Act
sections.content:
The sole legitimate forum to invalidate a fraudulent or coerced gift instrument is the Assistant Judge or Senior Assistant Judge Court. The lawsuit is instituted under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Suit for Cancellation of Document).

Statute of Limitations: Under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the lawsuit must be filed within 3 (three) years from the date the plaintiff discovers the fraudulent deed. Exceeding this 3-year deadline causes the claim to be barred by limitation. Concurrently, an application for temporary injunction under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 of the CPC must be pursued to freeze third-party alienation.
